name: Cervicomental angle surgery

lead: The cervicomental angle is the angle between the underside of the chin and the neck. A sharper, more defined angle is associated with a leaner, younger-looking jawline. Procedures that target it include liposuction of the submental fat, tightening of the platysma muscle, and neck lift surgery, sometimes with a facelift.

Non-surgical options also appear in studies: laser-assisted lipolysis, ultrasound and radiofrequency devices, and neurotoxin injections to the platysma bands. Published reports are mainly case series and reviews from plastic-surgery journals.

paras: Treatment is planned by a surgeon after assessing fat, muscle bands, skin laxity and bone structure. Options range from a short-scar neck lift through an incision under the chin, to extended facelift techniques, to device-based tightening. Recovery involves swelling and bruising, and outcomes are judged over months.

Complications from neck lift surgery reported in reviews include contour irregularities and expanding hematomas that need urgent surgical care. Results depend on anatomy and technique, and non-surgical methods have more limited tightening. A qualified plastic or facial plastic surgeon assesses suitability.

angle.text: These procedures change the contour under the chin. Surgeons describe a deeper, cleaner angle that makes the jawline and neck look more defined.

lead: Cervicomental angle surgery refers to procedures that deepen or define the angle between the chin and neck, usually by combining fat removal with work on the platysma muscle and skin. Reviews describe neck lift surgery, alone or with a facelift, as producing a more youthful cervicomental angle.[1]

For looks, the angle affects jawline definition and how lean the lower face appears. Surgical writing links it to jowling and neck banding; one review reports that an extended sub-SMAS facelift technique gave the best result in the author's opinion for neck rhytids, cervicomental angle and jawline definition.[2]

Less invasive routes include a short-scar neck lift through a submental incision with no skin removal,[3] microbotox to improve platysma apposition and contouring,[4] laser-assisted lipolysis,[5] and focused ultrasound or radiofrequency devices.[6][7]
infobox: Neck lift, liposuction, platysmaplasty, devices, neurotoxin

paras: A review of the aging neck explains the anatomy and physiology that surgeons use for planning, including fat, platysma bands and skin.[8] Platysma rejuvenation techniques are described in a review that also covers cervical rhytidectomy and complications.[9]

Extended SMAS and deep-plane approaches address the neck within a facelift.[2] A short-scar neck lift works through the submental incision, using deep layer changes while skin redistributes.[3] Reviews discuss the difficult neck in facelifting.[10]

Studies include HIFU for neck rejuvenation in 20 patients,[6] fractional radiofrequency microneedling with and without PRP in 20 patients,[11] a 1440 nm laser without liposuction,[12] laser-assisted lipolysis in 30 patients,[5] and HIFU with Q-switched laser.[7] Botulinum toxin neck work has anatomical guidelines published in 2024.[13]
A review of neck rejuvenation complications describes contour irregularities that may improve with time or need later surgery, and expanding hematomas needing immediate surgical intervention.[1]

Reported studies are small prospective series and randomized trials: HIFU in 20 patients,[6] RF microneedling alone versus with PRP in 20 randomized patients,[11] laser-assisted lipolysis in 30 patients,[5] and a 1440 nm laser study.[12] The surgical literature is mostly reviews and surgeon-reported technique descriptions.[1][2][3][9]
